extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, and typographers (especially University of Chicago Press staff)
extracted.subtask_description: A print-oriented manual of typographical style and composition rules used by the University of Chicago Press, covering capitalization, italics, headings, dates, titles, and specimen types with examples and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1. Proper nouns and adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize — 1. Proper nouns and adjectives: Geoige, America, North America, Englishman; Elizabethan, French. (See 53.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize verbs derived from proper names (to boycott, to fletcherize, to pasteurize), nor words used as electrical units (volt, ampere, watt, henry, ohm).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2. Epithets used as substitutes for proper names, or affixed to a name
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize epithets used as substitutes for proper names, or affixed to a name: the Pretender, Bloody Mary, Alexander the Great.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3. Particles in French and certain name particles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the particles in French names, as 'le,' 'la,' 'de,' 'du,' when they are not preceded by a Christian name or title; but do not capitalize them when they are preceded by such name or title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Bossu, La Torre, La Rochelle, De Coligny, D'Aubign^, Du Maurier (but: Ren^ le Bossu, Miguel de la Torre, Gaspard de Coligny, Thomas d'Aubign^, George du Maurier). Always capitalize 'Van' and 'Ten' in Dutch names; never capitalize 'von' in German names. Note: personal preference causes exceptions (Henry van Dyke, J. H. van't Hoff, Bernard E. C. ten Brink).

rubrics_metrics.name: 4. Generic terms forming part of geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize generic terms forming a part of geographical names such as Atlantic Ocean, Dead Sea, Baffin's Bay, Gulf of Mexico, Straits of Gibraltar, Mississippi River, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize words of this class when simply added by way of description to the specific name without forming an organic part: the river Elbe, the desert of Sahara, the island of Madagascar.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5. Adjectives and nouns used to distinguish definite regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize adjectives and nouns used singly or in conjunction to distinguish definite regions or parts of the world (Old World, Western Hemisphere, North Pole, the North (= Scandinavia), the East (the Orient), the Far East).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not, as a rule, capitalize adjectives derived from such names or nouns simply designating direction except as applied to geographical sections: oriental customs, the southern states (but Northern Asia, Continental Europe).

rubrics_metrics.name: 6. Generic terms for political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize generic terms for political divisions when they are an organic part of the name (Holy Roman Empire) or with 'of' as integral part (Department of the Lakes), when used singly as accepted designation (the Union), or when part of a fanciful/popular appellation (Celestial Empire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize such terms when standing alone or when with 'of' preceding the specific name in ordinary use: the empire, kingdom of Belgium, state of Illinois.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7. Numbered political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize numbered political divisions: Eleventh Congressional District, First Ward, Second Precinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (See 100 for related rules.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 8. Names of thoroughfares, parks, squares, blocks, buildings, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of thoroughfares, parks, squares, blocks, buildings: Drexel Avenue, Ringstrasse, Via Appia, Lincoln Park, Trafalgar Square, Monadnock Block, Lakeside Building, Capitol, White House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general designations like 'courthouse,' 'post-office,' 'library,' except in connection with the name of the place in which they are located.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9. Names of political parties, religious denominations, schools and adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of political parties, religious denominations or sects, and philosophical, literary, and artistic schools, and their adherents: Republican, Conservative, Christian, Protestantism, Evangelical Lutheran, Catholic, Epicurean, Stoic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize these words or their derivatives when used in a general sense (republican form of government, socialism as an economic panacea, pharisaic superciliousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: 10. Names of monastic orders and their members
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of monastic orders and their members: Black Friars, Dominican, Jesuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: 11. Proper (official) titles of organizations and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper (official) titles of social, religious, educational, political, commercial, and industrial organizations and institutions: Union League Club, Knights Templar, Smithsonian Institution, State University of Iowa, The Macmillan Company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic terms when designating a class or when standing alone (the club, the association, the company), unless used as a true name or to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12. Names of legislative, judiciary, administrative bodies and departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of legislative, judiciary, and administrative bodies and governmental departments, and their branches when specifically applied: Congress (Senate, House of Representatives), Parliament (House of Lords), Supreme Court of the United States, Department of the Interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general, paraphrastic, or incomplete designations: the national assembly, the legislature of the state, the council, the department.

rubrics_metrics.name: 13. Ordinals for dynasties, sessions, regiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize ordinals used to designate Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, names of regiments: the Eighteenth Dynasty, the Fifty-third Congress, the Second Illinois Regiment Band.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14. Appellations for historical epochs, literary periods, geological ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize commonly accepted appellations for historical epochs, periods in language or literature, and geological ages (Stone age, Crusades, Renaissance, Middle Ages, Pleistocene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'age' is capitalized only where failure to do so would be ambiguous (Stone age but Middle Ages).

rubrics_metrics.name: 15. Names for important events
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names for important events: Thirty Years' War, Revolutionary War or War of Independence (American), Battle of Gettysburg, Peace of Utrecht.

rubrics_metrics.name: 16. Political alliances and historically significant party/movement terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize political alliances and terms from secular or ecclesiastical history that have acquired special significance: Protestant League, Holy Alliance, Dreibund; the Roses, the Roundheads, Independents.

rubrics_metrics.name: 17. Conventions, congresses, expositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize conventions, congresses, expositions and similar gatherings: Council of Nicaea, Parliament of Religions, Fifteenth International Congress of Criminology, Chicago World's Fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18. Titles of treaties, acts, laws, bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of specific treaties, acts, laws, bills: Treaty of Verdun, Art. V of the Peace of Prague, Edict of Nantes, Concordat, the Constitution (of the United States when standing alone), Declaration of Independence, Fourteenth Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not usually capitalize constitution when not referring to the U.S. Constitution specifically (the constitution of Illinois).

rubrics_metrics.name: 19. Creeds and confessions of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize creeds and confessions of faith: Apostles' Creed, Nicene Creed, Augsburg Confession, Thirty-nine Articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize adjectives derived from such nouns (biblical, scriptural).

rubrics_metrics.name: 20. Civic holidays and ecclesiastical fast and feast days
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize civic holidays and ecclesiastical fast and feast days: Fourth of July (the Fourth), Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day; Easter, Passover, Feast of Tabernacles, New Year's Day.

rubrics_metrics.name: 21. Titles of honor and respect preceding the name
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of honor and respect, whether religious, civil, or military, preceding the name, and academic degrees in abbreviated form following the name: Queen Victoria, Rear-Admiral Dewey, Timothy Dwight, DD., LL.D.; the Prince of Wales, His Majesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize official title when it follows the name (McKinley, president of the United States) or when standing alone without referring to the existing incumbent (the emperor of Germany), except certain exceptions noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 22. Abbreviations like Ph.D., M.P., F.R.G.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize abbreviations like Ph.D., M.P., and F.R.G.S. (set without space between the letters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize such phrases when spelled out (doctor of philosophy), with some cross-references to other rules (see 52, 103, 106).

rubrics_metrics.name: 23. One-letter abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize abbreviations consisting of one letter only, except in case of units of measurement and minor literary subdivisions: R.V. (Revised Version), C. (centigrade), L.C.M. (lowest common multiple), H.P. (horse-power), A (angstrom units).

rubrics_metrics.name: 24. Nouns and adjectives designating the Supreme Being or Trinty
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns and adjectives used to designate the Supreme Being or Power, or any member of the Christian Trinity; and all pronouns referring to the same, when not closely preceded or followed by a distinctive name: the Almighty, Providence, Father, Son, Holy Ghost, the Logos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize derived expressions like (God's) fatherhood, messiahship, messianic. Also see exception for 'When God had worked six days...' which retains sentence case for biblical narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: 25. Words with acquired, limited, or special meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words which have an acquired, limited, or special meaning: the Doctor's degree; a report of the Master (in chancery); a Bachelor's hood; a Freshman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize the corresponding general expressions: the doctorate, a master in chancery.

rubrics_metrics.name: 26. Personified concepts like 'Nature'
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Nature' and similar terms, and abstract ideas, when personified: 'Nature wields her scepter mercilessly'; 'Vice in the old English morality plays.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 27. 'Father' for church father and 'Reformers' for Reformation leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Father' used for church father, and 'Reformers' used of Reformation leaders, whenever the meaning otherwise would be ambiguous: the Fathers, the early Fathers, the Greek Fathers, the Reformers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize when context indicates the generic church reformers of the fifteenth century; use lower-case in those ordinary senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: 28. The word 'church' in properly cited titles of bodies or edifices
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Church' in properly cited titles of nationally organized bodies of believers inseparably linked with a locality, or when forming part of an edifice name: Church of Rome, Church of England, Fifth Avenue Baptist Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize 'church' when standing alone in universal, national, local, or incomplete citations: the church (organized Christianity), the Roman Catholic church; but 'the Establishment' is capitalized in certain senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: 29. Names for the Bible and other sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names for the Bible and other sacred books: (Holy, Sacred) Scriptures, Holy Writ, Word of God, Book of Books; Koran, Vedas, Mishna, Upanishads; Apocrypha.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize adjectives derived from such nouns (biblical, scriptural, koranic).

rubrics_metrics.name: 30. Versions of the Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize versions of the Bible: King James's Version, Authorized Version (A.V.), Revised Version (R.V.), Polychrome Bible, Septuagint (LXX), Peshitto.

rubrics_metrics.name: 31. Books and divisions of the Bible and other sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize books and divisions of the Bible and other sacred books: Old Testament, Pentateuch, Exodus, Second Kings, Book of Job, Psalms, Gospel of Luke, Acts of the Apostles, Epistle to the Romans, Apocalypse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize words like 'book,' 'gospel,' 'epistle,' 'psalm' in phrases such as the five books of Moses, the first forty psalms, the gospels and epistles of the New Testament.

rubrics_metrics.name: 32. Biblical parables
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize biblical parables: the parable of the Prodigal Son.

rubrics_metrics.name: 33. Miscellaneous biblical or ecclesiastical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize such miscellaneous terms as Last Supper, Eucharist, the Passion, the Twelve (apostles), the Seventy (disciples), the Servant, the Day of Yahweh, the Chronicler, the Psalmist, the Golden Rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 34. First word of a sentence and first word of each line in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a sentence, and in poetry the first word of each line. (In Greek and Latin poetry capitalize only the first word of a paragraph, not each verse.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples of English poetry and notes about Greek/Latin exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35. First word after a colon (conditional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word after a colon only when introducing a complete passage or sentence that would have independent meaning, as in summarizations and quotations not closely connected with what precedes; or where the colon has the weight of 'as follows' or 'namely.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize after a colon when the quotation is immediately connected with what precedes, or when the colon introduces a phrase logically dependent on the preceding clause, or where it signals a note of comment. Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 36. First word in sections of enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, capitalize the first word in sections of enumeration if any one link contains two or more distinct clauses (not in parentheses) separated by semicolon, colon, or period, unless all are dependent upon the same preceding term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrating when to capitalize based on clause independence and punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37. Nouns followed by a numeral indicating order
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, capitalize nouns followed by a numeral indicating their order in a sequence: Room 16, Ps. 30, Grade IV, Act I, Vol. I, No. 3, Book II, Part IV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize minor subdivisions like sec. 4, scene i, art. iii, chap. 2 when treated as minor subdivisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 38. First word of a cited speech in direct discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a cited speech (thought) in direct discourse, whether preceded by a colon or a comma: On leaving he remarked: 'Never shall I forget this day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also covers presentation when quotation marks are omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 39. First words in resolutions following 'Whereas' and 'Resolved'
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first words following 'Whereas' and 'Resolved' in resolutions: Whereas, It has pleased God...; therefore be it Resolved, That....

rubrics_metrics.name: 40. The exclamations 'O' and 'Oh'
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the exclamations 'O' and 'Oh': 'O Lord!' 'Oh, that I were home again!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also rule 117 cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: 41. Principal words in English titles of publications and divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize all the principal words (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, verbs, first and last words) in English titles of publications and their divisions, subjects of lectures, cap-and-small-cap and italic center-heads, bold-face cut-in heads and side-heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes botanical and bibliography exceptions where only first words and proper names may be capitalized. See 279-283 for table headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 42. Capitalization in foreign titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In foreign titles, in addition to capitalizing the first word, follow language-specific rules: (a) Latin: capitalize proper nouns and adjectives derived therefrom; (b) French/Italian/Spanish/Swedish/Norwegian: capitalize proper nouns but not derived adjectives; (c) German/Danish: capitalize all nouns but not adjectives (except German adjectives derived from proper names); (d) Dutch: capitalize all nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each language.

rubrics_metrics.name: 43. Definite article with newspapers and magazines
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, as a rule, treat the definite article as part of the title of newspapers and magazines: the Chicago Tribune, the School Review.

rubrics_metrics.name: 44. Titles of ancient manuscripts (MS, MSS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of ancient manuscripts: Codex Bemensis, Cod. Canonicianus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 60 for related rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 45. Hyphenated compounds in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with the main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds: 'Twentieth-Century Progress,' 'The Economy of High-Speed Trains.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize components when other than nouns: Fifty-first Street, 'Lives of Well-known Authors.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 46. Scientific (Latin) names capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera in botanical, geological, zoological, and paleontological matter, but not their English derivatives: Cotylosauria (but cotylosaurs), Felidae (but felids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names of species derived from persons or from generic names may be capitalized in botanical and zoological matter; in geological and medical matter species names are not capitalized. Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes: Kafir, Negro (in its ethnical sense), Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials.

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Names of bodies in the solar system
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of the bodies of our solar system (except 'sun,' 'earth,' 'moon,' 'stars'): the Milky Way, the Great Bear, Saturn.

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. University of Chicago internal divisions and officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University of Chicago in official work dealing with its administration or curricula: the School of Education (the School), the Department of Anthropology (but: the department); the Board of Trustees, the Senate, the President, the Registrar, Professor of Physics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes differences between official and generic usage (the division, the department, the faculty) and use of capitals/small capitals for certain address and signature formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Use of capitals and small capitals in letter headings and signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Capitals and Small Capitals for the names of town and state in the date line, salutatory phrase, signature and residence at the end of letters or articles: Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1911; My dear Mr. Smith:; Charles W. Scott; Harvard University, Cambridge, Mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting guidance: set to the right with specified indentation and type size; address lines in caps and small caps and centered on preceding lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. 'Whereas', 'Note', and 'Section' formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions, the word 'Whereas' is set in caps (see 39); in notes (not footnotes) the word 'Note' is used followed by a period and dash; in constitutions/by-laws 'Section' introduces paragraphs and is followed by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usual practice is to abbreviate 'section' after the first occurrence: Section 1. The name...; Sec. 2. The object...

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Use of small capitals for certain abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M. and P.M. (ante- and post-meridiem) and B.C. and A.D. (before Christ and anno Domini) in small capitals and without a space between letters: 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C., 1906 A.D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rules 22, 103, 106, 219.

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Use small initial letter for formerly proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use small initial letter for words of common usage originally proper names whose origin has become obscured, and generally all verbs derived from proper names: Utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, boycott, roman (type), italicize.

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Lower-case for literary subdivisions and abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case for minor literary subdivisions and their abbreviations in references: chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note; chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 37, 110, and 337 for related use.

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Units of measurement (abbreviations) in lower case
rubrics_metrics.description: Set units of measurement in small (lower-case) initial letters: h.=hour, min.=minute, sec.=second; lb.=pound, oz.=ounce; yd.=yard, ft.=foot; etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. Italic side-heads capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper names; set all other words in lower case (see 172 and 280).

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. First word of a quotation connected with preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a quotation which, through a conjunction or otherwise, is immediately connected with what precedes, even if that word in the original begins a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 35 and 131 for illustration and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Italics for emphasis and importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to which it is desired to lend emphasis, importance, etc.: 'This was, however, not the case'; 'It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life, at least, are studies of processes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Italics for foreign words and brief foreign passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words and phrases from foreign languages inserted into the English text and not incorporated into English; also (as a rule) single sentences or brief passages not of sufficient length to call for reduced type: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung'; 'Napoleon's coup d'état'; 'De gustibus non est disputandum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names, names of foreign institutions or places whose English equivalents exist or are used, nor words of everyday occurrence that are sufficiently anglicized (percent, personnel, attaché, façade).
